extracted.intended_audience: students, intellectuals, and policymakers interested in American democratic theory and foreign policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting normative criteria for what constitutes a proper national democracy and national foreign policy — including standards for sovereignty, legislation, protest, organization, and the prudent application of doctrines like the Monroe Doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional justification of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: All rights under the law are functions in a democratic political organism and must be justified by their actual or presumable functional adequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal rights should not be treated as sacred abstractions; each right must be defensible in terms of how it aids the democratic political organism. The implication is to evaluate laws by their practical contribution to the national democratic purpose rather than by ritual deference to precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive relation of national organization to democratic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The American national political organization should be constructively related to their democratic purpose; the Constitution and legal fabric must be modifiable to serve a comprehensive democratic aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'superstitious awe' toward the Constitution or legal precedent that prevents necessary change. The text warns against worship of legal precedent 'for its own sake' and promotes adapting institutions so they serve a 'lofty and far-reaching democratic purpose.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular (national) sovereignty as collective purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The people are Sovereign only insofar as they succeed in reaching and expressing a collective purpose; popular sovereignty is equivalent to national sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereignty is not simply the act of any chance majority; it requires fullness and consistency of national life and an expression of collective will. Evaluations should ask whether a purported exercise of 'popular sovereignty' truly reflects a coherent national purpose rather than transient majority advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule is necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Majority rule, under prescribed conditions, is a necessary constituent of democratic organization, but the actions of a majority need not have binding moral or national authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat majority decisions as procedural machinery rather than automatic moral or national validation. Check for safeguards (tradition, fundamental law, deliberation) that convert majority action into morally authoritative policy; beware of accepting mere numerical majorities as definitively sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demanded sacrifices must serve the national purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Sacrifices of tradition and interest can only be demanded in case they contribute to the national purpose — the gradual creation of a higher type of individual and associated life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy makers should justify costs imposed on groups by showing those costs genuinely further the national democratic ideal. The text emphasizes mitigation of friction by 'mutual loyalty and good faith' and insists on connecting sacrifice to demonstrable contribution to national aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for legitimate protest
rubrics_metrics.description: Protests against national policy must not refuse obedience to the law; private interests injured must show injuries unnecessary or that they involve harm to an essential public interest; protests must find ultimate sanction in constructive democratic ideas and not be used as excuses for personal injustice or national disloyalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators of protest should demand procedural respect (no lawlessness), substantive demonstration of harm or injustice, and alignment with constructive democratic principles. The passage allows for 'vivacious and persistent' protest but insists on patient good faith and that protest not devolve into personal or disloyal attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of organization and institutionalization for social reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious faith or moral impulse alone cannot realize lasting social/political reform; faith must be established by habit, defined by thought, and consolidated by organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: expecting immediate, miraculous societal conversion (Tolstoyan non-resistance). Good practice: build durable institutions, habits, and disciplined organization to translate ideals into stable social gains. The text notes that movements lacking such organization 'must in a worldly sense inevitably perish.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of coercion as part of national schooling
rubrics_metrics.description: The exigencies of national schooling frequently demand severe coercive measures; a nation cannot merely discharge its unregenerate citizens and must sometimes use compulsion to maintain social order and achieve democratic ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coercion is framed as a pragmatic tool within an organized national education and discipline system. Evaluations should weigh whether coercive measures are proportionate, pedagogically justified, and tied to the nationalizing and ameliorating aims described, not arbitrary or oppressive ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: National organization as comprehensive basis for association
rubrics_metrics.description: National organization provides a basis of association that guarantees protection against predatory powers, provides for individual freedom, discipline, and social consistency, and offers both prizes and coercion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional arrangements by whether they balance protection, liberty, discipline, and social cohesion. The nation is praised for encompassing the 'whole complex of human powers and interests' and for being the plausible framework for achieving democratic brotherhood in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual insight and patriotic candor in diagnosing national ills
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual loyalty must be reinforced by the intelligence to trace national ills to their causes and the candid courage to advocate necessary remedial measures; the national school demands training in the ability to draw inferences from national experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy evaluation should include careful historical and factual analysis ('close and exact reading' of national experience). Leaders and citizens should be judged on their capacity for disinterested, critical appraisal and for proposing remedies — not merely on partisan loyalty or rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign policy must be candidly national and based on national interest aligned with democratic ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuinely national foreign policy must be based upon a correct understanding of the national interest in relation to neighbors and must unite national efficiency with democratic idealism; the United States must assume a definite and responsible place in the international system as its nationality deepens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign-policy proposals should be tested for (a) fidelity to a clear conception of national interest, (b) consistency with democratic principles (encouraging spread of democratic methods where practicable), and (c) willingness to accept increasing international ties and duties as a natural consequence of a robust nationality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence in applying the Monroe Doctrine (avoid rigid continental isolationism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Monroe Doctrine was originally justified as protection against European intervention in American independence movements, but its rigid, militant application risks committing the United States to unrighteous wars and inappropriate aggression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate invocation of the Monroe Doctrine by asking whether it (1) defends genuine national-democratic interests, (2) prudently distinguishes territorial aggression from ordinary economic and demographic ties (migration, investment), and (3) avoids promising war in cases where European involvement might be justifiable under international law. The passage recommends modifying the Doctrine into a positive, practicable principle rather than an absolutist slogan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish military capability from righteousness of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition and enforcement of a foreign-policy proclamation (like the Monroe Doctrine) depend on military/naval power, but the crucial question is whether a doctrine risks committing the nation to a war that would be unrighteous — opposing legitimate interests of other nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should not equate the capacity to compel recognition with moral justification. When preparing for or threatening force, they must evaluate the justice of the cause and whether conflict would oppose a legitimate foreign interest; mere ability to fight does not validate a policy.
